status: Original educational questions, Batch 03; 61 new exam-style questions pending independent clinical editorial verification. Not official RCOG/Egyptian Fellowship exam material.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman at 12 weeks has a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect. Which folic acid regimen is most appropriate in a future planned pregnancy?
options: 400 micrograms daily from 12 weeks
5 mg daily from before conception until 12 weeks
5 mg daily only after the anomaly scan
400 micrograms weekly until delivery
No supplementation if diet is adequate
questions.rationale: A previous neural tube defect-affected pregnancy is a high-risk indication for high-dose folic acid before conception and through the first trimester. Confirm the exact current local guideline before prescribing.
questions.traps: Routine 400 microgram dosing is intended for lower-risk pregnancies; starting at 12 weeks misses the key neural tube closure window.

questions.stem: A haemodynamically unstable patient has a positive pregnancy test, abdominal pain and suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy. What is the immediate priority?
options: Repeat serum hCG in 48 hours
Arrange outpatient ultrasound
Immediate resuscitation and urgent surgical assessment
Give methotrexate
Discharge with safety-netting
questions.rationale: Maternal stabilisation and urgent operative assessment take precedence over serial investigations in suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
questions.traps: Methotrexate and serial hCG are inappropriate for instability.

questions.stem: A woman with eclampsia has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Which drug is first-line to prevent recurrent seizures?
options: Diazepam
Phenytoin
Magnesium sulfate
Sodium valproate
Levetiracetam
questions.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is first-line for prevention and treatment of recurrent eclamptic seizures, alongside stabilisation and delivery planning.
questions.traps: Other anticonvulsants are not preferred first-line in eclampsia.

questions.stem: Immediately after birth a woman has heavy vaginal bleeding and a boggy enlarged uterus. What is the most likely primary cause?
options: Uterine inversion
Uterine atony
Cervical laceration
Retained vaginal pack
Amniotic fluid embolism
questions.rationale: A boggy uterus with immediate postpartum haemorrhage strongly suggests uterine atony; initiate the local PPH protocol immediately.
questions.traps: Trauma often causes bleeding despite a well-contracted uterus.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with postmenopausal bleeding. What is the most important diagnosis to exclude?
options: Endometrial carcinoma
Mittelschmerz
Primary dysmenorrhoea
Physiological ovulation
Pelvic inflammatory disease
questions.rationale: Postmenopausal bleeding requires assessment to exclude endometrial malignancy, even though benign causes are common.
questions.traps: Do not dismiss bleeding as atrophy without appropriate assessment.

questions.stem: A patient with a current breast cancer diagnosis requests contraception. Which option is generally most appropriate?
options: Combined oral contraceptive
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system
Copper intrauterine device
Progestogen-only implant
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate
questions.rationale: A non-hormonal copper IUD is generally preferred where suitable in current breast cancer; assess individual contraindications.
questions.traps: Hormonal methods are generally contraindicated in current breast cancer.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes wants to conceive this month. HbA1c is 92 mmol/mol (10.6%). She has background retinopathy and takes ramipril for albuminuria. Which integrated plan is most appropriate?
options: Begin trying now with folic acid 5 mg and arrange a scan at 6 weeks
Continue ramipril until a pregnancy test is positive and then stop it
Advise postponement of conception, optimise glycaemia, assess retinal and renal disease, review ramipril and prescribe folic acid 5 mg
Replace insulin with metformin and start aspirin before conception
Proceed with conception if fasting glucose readings are normal despite the HbA1c
questions.rationale: NICE NG3 advises against conception with HbA1c >86 mmol/mol; aim <48 if safely achievable. Preconception folate 5 mg and complication/medication review are required.
questions.traps: A few normal capillary values do not override high HbA1c; folate does not neutralise uncontrolled diabetes.

questions.stem: A woman with chronic hypertension and a previous delivery at 29 weeks for severe pre-eclampsia plans pregnancy. She is taking losartan. Blood pressure is 142/92 mmHg. What is the most appropriate strategy?
options: Stop all antihypertensives now and begin aspirin immediately
Continue losartan until fetal cardiac activity is confirmed
Replace losartan with a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive while controlling BP, arrange risk assessment, and plan aspirin from 12 weeks
Start low-molecular-weight heparin before conception to prevent recurrence
Recommend pregnancy only if all antihypertensive medication can be discontinued
questions.rationale: Avoid ARBs in planned pregnancy and maintain maternal BP control; NICE NG133 recommends aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks for high-risk women.
questions.traps: Do not confuse preconception medication optimisation with the timing of aspirin prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A woman with type 2 diabetes and an HbA1c of 49 mmol/mol is taking metformin and gliclazide. She is planning pregnancy and asks whether her current tablets can simply be continued. Which advice best reflects UK guidance?
options: Both drugs should always be continued unchanged
Stop metformin and use gliclazide alone
Metformin may be continued if benefits outweigh potential harm, but gliclazide should be stopped before pregnancy and insulin used if needed
Stop all glucose-lowering treatment until the first antenatal appointment
Gliclazide is preferred to insulin because it avoids injections
questions.rationale: NICE NG3 permits metformin when benefits outweigh potential harm; other oral glucose-lowering agents should be stopped before pregnancy and insulin substituted as indicated.
questions.traps: Metformin is not treated identically to every other oral hypoglycaemic.

questions.stem: A woman with chronic hypertension becomes pregnant unexpectedly at 5 weeks while taking an ACE inhibitor. She is asymptomatic and BP is 150/96 mmHg. Which is the best next step?
options: Continue ACE inhibitor until 12 weeks because organogenesis is not complete
Stop the ACE inhibitor promptly and arrange an appropriate pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive with clinical review
Stop every BP drug and reassess only at 20 weeks
Begin aspirin 300 mg immediately instead of an antihypertensive
Reassure her that no medication review is needed unless ultrasound is abnormal
questions.rationale: ACE inhibitors/ARBs require prompt review in pregnancy, while hypertension should remain controlled using an appropriate alternative.
questions.traps: Stopping the teratogenic drug does not mean leaving clinically important hypertension untreated.

questions.stem: A woman with type 1 diabetes and hypoglycaemia unawareness is trying to reach HbA1c 6.5% before conception. She has repeated severe hypoglycaemia at night. What is the best counselling?
options: Insist on HbA1c <6.5% regardless of hypoglycaemia
Aim for the lowest HbA1c achievable without problematic hypoglycaemia and optimise specialist support
Stop basal insulin to avoid nocturnal episodes
Conception is safe as long as HbA1c is under 10%
Use urine glucose instead of capillary monitoring
questions.rationale: The preconception HbA1c target is conditional on avoiding problematic hypoglycaemia. Specialist adjustment and monitoring are essential.
questions.traps: Numerical targets must not override maternal safety.

questions.stem: A stable woman presents at approximately 5 weeks with mild unilateral pain. Transvaginal ultrasound shows neither an intrauterine nor an ectopic pregnancy. Serum hCG rises from 900 to 1,530 IU/L in 48 hours. What is the best interpretation and plan?
options: This rise proves a viable intrauterine pregnancy and excludes ectopic pregnancy
This rise proves ectopic pregnancy because the uterus is empty
Likely developing intrauterine pregnancy, but ectopic remains possible; arrange follow-up TVUS and safety-netting
Perform uterine evacuation solely to establish the pregnancy location
Discharge permanently without further assessment because the rise exceeds 63%
questions.rationale: The rise is 70%. NICE NG126 indicates likely developing IUP but ectopic cannot be excluded; arrange TVUS 7–14 days later, consider earlier if hCG >=1500, and provide emergency precautions.
questions.traps: hCG trends assess proliferation, not location.

questions.stem: A woman with a pregnancy of unknown location has hCG 1,600 IU/L followed 48 hours later by 1,950 IU/L. She is clinically stable. Which next action is most appropriate under NICE guidance?
options: Reassure and book a scan in 14 days without review
Diagnose viable intrauterine pregnancy
Refer for clinical review in the early pregnancy assessment service within 24 hours
Diagnose miscarriage from the suboptimal rise
Use serum progesterone as the definitive test of pregnancy location
questions.rationale: The rise is below 63%; NICE recommends clinical review within 24 hours for a rise <63% or fall <50%.
questions.traps: A plateauing hCG does not establish the pregnancy location.

questions.stem: At 6 weeks by uncertain dates, a woman has a transvaginal scan showing an intrauterine embryo with CRL 6.2 mm and no cardiac activity. She has no bleeding or pain. What is the best management?
options: Diagnose missed miscarriage immediately
Give misoprostol the same day
Repeat TVUS at least 7 days later before diagnosing pregnancy loss
Repeat ultrasound in 24 hours and diagnose miscarriage if unchanged
Use one serum hCG level to establish non-viability
questions.rationale: For CRL <7 mm with absent heartbeat on TVUS, NICE NG126 requires a repeat scan after at least 7 days.
questions.traps: Do not apply thresholds as if they were automatic grounds for immediate irreversible treatment.

questions.stem: A woman with a positive pregnancy test, severe unilateral pain, syncope and shoulder-tip pain arrives hypotensive. A previous hCG result was 680 IU/L and a prior scan showed no intrauterine pregnancy. What is the best immediate action?
options: Repeat hCG in 48 hours before deciding
Give oral analgesia and arrange routine ultrasound in one week
Urgent resuscitation, senior gynaecology assessment and emergency management of suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Diagnose a biochemical pregnancy because hCG is below 1,500
Request serum progesterone before considering surgery
questions.rationale: Clinical instability overrides hCG thresholds; a ruptured ectopic must be managed as an emergency.
questions.traps: The discriminatory zone is not a haemodynamic safety threshold.

questions.stem: A woman with PUL has hCG 2,400 IU/L, falling to 960 IU/L after 48 hours. She is asymptomatic and has clear return precautions. Which follow-up is most appropriate under NICE?
options: No follow-up because ectopic pregnancy is excluded
Urine pregnancy test 14 days after the second serum hCG, with review if positive
Routine laparoscopy in every patient with a falling hCG
Repeat hCG every 6 hours until negative
Give methotrexate immediately
questions.rationale: A fall >50% suggests pregnancy unlikely to continue but does not confirm resolution; NICE recommends urine pregnancy test after 14 days and review if positive.
questions.traps: Falling hCG does not by itself exclude an ectopic.

questions.stem: At booking, a nulliparous 41-year-old woman has BMI 36 kg/m2, normal BP and no chronic disease. Which prophylaxis best follows NICE NG133?
options: No aspirin because she has no previous pre-eclampsia
Aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth
Aspirin 300 mg daily from booking until 20 weeks
Low-molecular-weight heparin alone to prevent pre-eclampsia
Start aspirin only if hypertension develops
questions.rationale: She has multiple moderate risk factors (nulliparity, age >=40, BMI >=35), meeting NICE aspirin criteria.
questions.traps: One moderate factor alone differs from >1 moderate factors.

questions.stem: At 30 weeks a low-risk singleton pregnancy has fundal height crossing down two centile lines, with no prior growth scans. The mother reports normal fetal movements and BP is normal. What is the best next investigation?
options: No investigation because movements are normal
Offer ultrasound assessment of fetal growth and wellbeing
Start twice-weekly CTG without ultrasound
Diagnose fetal growth restriction from fundal height alone
Plan delivery at 32 weeks without confirming growth
questions.rationale: NICE NG201 recommends ultrasound if SFH is small for gestational age; urgency depends on other clinical findings.
questions.traps: SFH is a screening tool, not a definitive FGR diagnosis.

questions.stem: A woman at 29 weeks with an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy asks for fortnightly ultrasound growth scans because her friend had an undiagnosed small baby. Her SFH chart is appropriate and there are no risk factors. What is the most guideline-consistent approach?
options: Offer fortnightly growth scans to all women after 28 weeks
Offer routine 4-weekly umbilical artery Doppler
Continue routine care and serial SFH at appropriate visits, reassessing risk if new findings arise
Diagnose placental insufficiency from the family anecdote
Schedule induction at 37 weeks
questions.rationale: NICE NG201 advises against routine scans after 28 weeks in uncomplicated singleton pregnancies; SFH is assessed after 24 weeks, not more often than every 2 weeks.
questions.traps: More testing is not always better care in a low-risk pregnancy.

questions.stem: At 28 weeks, a woman with chronic hypertension on labetalol has repeated BP 146/94 mmHg. She has no severe features and normal initial blood tests. Which UK-guideline target is most appropriate while adjusting medication?
options: Aim for 100/60 mmHg in all cases
Aim for 135/85 mmHg while avoiding symptomatic hypotension
Do not treat unless BP exceeds 160/110 mmHg
Stop labetalol and use an ARB
Use aspirin as the sole antihypertensive
questions.rationale: NICE NG133 recommends target BP 135/85 mmHg in treated chronic hypertension during pregnancy.
questions.traps: Aspirin is preventive, not a substitute for BP control.

questions.stem: At a routine 26-week appointment a woman says fetal movements have been clearly reduced since yesterday. Her SFH is on the expected centile and BP is normal. What is the best response?
options: Reassure because SFH is normal
Advise waiting until the next scheduled visit
Arrange assessment of mother and fetus now according to the local reduced fetal movements pathway
Advise home counting for one week before contacting services
Order a growth scan in 4 weeks without current assessment
questions.rationale: NICE NG201 advises assessment whenever reduced fetal movements are reported after 24 weeks.
questions.traps: Normal SFH cannot exclude acute fetal compromise.

questions.stem: A woman with pre-existing type 1 diabetes attends at 10 weeks. HbA1c at booking is 58 mmol/mol. She asks whether HbA1c should replace capillary glucose testing throughout pregnancy. What is the best response?
options: Use HbA1c alone weekly throughout pregnancy
Use capillary/CGM glucose management; booking HbA1c helps risk assessment but is not the routine tool for second- and third-trimester control
Stop glucose monitoring after the anomaly scan
Measure urine glucose only
HbA1c at booking has no clinical role
questions.rationale: NICE NG3 uses booking HbA1c for risk assessment but advises against routine HbA1c for glycaemic control in the second and third trimesters.
questions.traps: A useful risk marker is not necessarily a suitable day-to-day treatment monitor.

questions.stem: At booking a woman reports previous admission for pulmonary embolism after major surgery and is currently pregnant. Which principle is most appropriate for antenatal planning?
options: VTE risk is assessed only after delivery
Document an individual VTE risk assessment at booking and reassess after admissions or significant health events, with specialist prophylaxis planning
Start aspirin alone and omit VTE risk assessment
Reassess only if she develops leg swelling
Ignore provoked prior VTE because it cannot recur
questions.rationale: NICE NG201 calls for VTE risk assessment at booking and after hospital admission or significant events; treatment decisions require risk-specific guidance.
questions.traps: A previous provoked VTE still warrants careful risk stratification; aspirin is not routine VTE prophylaxis.

questions.stem: At the 12-week booking visit a woman declines infectious disease screening after a detailed discussion. She understands the implications and has decision-making capacity. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Perform tests without consent because screening is mandatory
Document informed refusal, provide balanced information and revisit if she wishes
Discharge her from antenatal care
Ask her partner to provide consent instead
Inform her that refusal makes all other screening unavailable
questions.rationale: NICE NG201 states women can accept or decline components of offered screening programmes; informed consent and continuing care remain essential.
questions.traps: Screening is offered, not imposed.

questions.stem: A woman with type 1 diabetes, HbA1c 49 mmol/mol, normal renal function and treated proliferative retinopathy wishes to conceive. She uses insulin and atorvastatin. She has already commenced folic acid 5 mg. What is the most appropriate next action?
options: Proceed without changing medication because HbA1c is near target
Stop insulin and start metformin
Review and discontinue atorvastatin before pregnancy while optimising glucose and arranging retinal follow-up
Delay pregnancy until HbA1c is below 30 mmol/mol
Give aspirin before conception instead of reviewing medicines
questions.rationale: Near-target HbA1c does not make statins suitable in pregnancy; preconception medication and retinal review remain necessary.
questions.traps: A numerically good HbA1c is not a substitute for teratogenic medication review.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old with chronic hypertension controlled on losartan plans conception. She has no albuminuria or other comorbidity. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Continue losartan throughout the first trimester
Switch to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive before conception and reassess blood pressure
Stop all treatment and ignore BP until 20 weeks
Replace losartan with spironolactone
Add methotrexate to reduce fetal risks
questions.rationale: Angiotensin receptor blockers should be avoided when planning pregnancy; select a pregnancy-compatible alternative and monitor BP.
questions.traps: Do not equate excellent BP control with medication safety.
questions.sourceDate: Guideline recommendations accessed 2026-11-25; original recommendation dates shown on source page

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with previous severe pre-eclampsia at 29 weeks is planning a second pregnancy. She asks whether low-dose aspirin should start immediately before conception. Which is the best UK-guideline response?
options: Begin 150 mg aspirin six months before conception
Begin aspirin only after proteinuria develops
Plan aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks in the next pregnancy, alongside preconception risk assessment
Avoid aspirin because pre-eclampsia was early onset
Use prophylactic LMWH instead of aspirin for all such women
questions.rationale: NICE recommends 75–150 mg aspirin daily from 12 weeks for previous hypertensive disease in pregnancy; preconception review remains important.
questions.traps: High-risk status determines aspirin indication, not routine preconception aspirin timing.
questions.sourceDate: Guideline recommendations accessed 2026-11-25; original recommendation dates shown on source page

questions.stem: A woman with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria is planning pregnancy. HbA1c is 72 mmol/mol. She asks whether switching from an ACE inhibitor to labetalol alone makes conception safe. Which is the best response?
options: Yes, antihypertensive substitution removes the major fetal risks
Yes, provided urine ketones are negative
No: optimise glycaemia, assess renal and retinal status, review all medication and provide high-dose folate before trying
No: pregnancy is permanently contraindicated in any microalbuminuria
Start an SGLT2 inhibitor and conceive next week
questions.rationale: Preconception risk reduction requires integrated glucose, renal, retinal and drug review; medication switching alone is inadequate.
questions.traps: Single-intervention distractor: fixing one risk does not address cumulative maternal-fetal risk.
questions.sourceDate: Guideline recommendations accessed 2026-11-25; original recommendation dates shown on source page
questions.sourceVerification: Official primary guideline; requires final clinical editorial review

questions.stem: A nulliparous 40-year-old woman with BMI 36 kg/m² plans pregnancy. She has no chronic disease. At 10 weeks in a subsequent singleton pregnancy, what is the most appropriate prophylaxis plan under NICE?
options: No aspirin unless hypertension develops
Aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks because she has more than one moderate-risk factor
Aspirin 300 mg daily from 10 weeks
LMWH for the entire pregnancy as the first-line pre-eclampsia prevention
Aspirin only if an abnormal uterine artery Doppler appears
questions.rationale: Nulliparity, age ≥40 and BMI ≥35 are moderate-risk factors; more than one qualifies for aspirin from 12 weeks.
questions.traps: One moderate factor is not the same as more than one.
questions.sourceDate: Guideline recommendations accessed 2026-11-25; original recommendation dates shown on source page

questions.stem: A 27-year-old with PUL has hCG 820 IU/L, then 1,420 IU/L at 48 hours. She now develops severe unilateral pain and shoulder-tip pain, with BP 88/54 mmHg. What is the best immediate action?
options: Reassure because hCG rose by more than 63%
Repeat hCG in another 48 hours
Urgent resuscitation and immediate senior surgical assessment for suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Give outpatient methotrexate immediately
Repeat TVUS in 14 days
questions.rationale: Clinical deterioration overrides apparently reassuring hCG kinetics; treat possible rupture urgently.
questions.traps: A >63% rise does not establish intrauterine location.
questions.sourceDate: Guideline recommendations accessed 2026-11-25; original recommendation dates shown on source page

questions.stem: A clinically well woman with PUL has hCG 1,600 IU/L followed by 680 IU/L 48 hours later, with no pain and reliable follow-up. What is the best NICE-based plan?
options: Discharge without safety-net advice because ectopic pregnancy is excluded
Arrange urine pregnancy test 14 days after the second hCG and provide emergency return advice
Administer methotrexate routinely
Arrange immediate laparoscopy despite absence of symptoms
Start progesterone to confirm intrauterine pregnancy
questions.rationale: A fall >50% suggests a pregnancy unlikely to continue; advise a urine test after 14 days and urgent review if positive or symptoms develop.
questions.traps: A steep fall does not prove pregnancy location or entirely exclude ectopic complications.

questions.stem: A stable woman with PUL has serum hCG 1,250 IU/L and 1,470 IU/L after 48 hours. She has mild intermittent pain and no definitive adnexal mass. What is the best next step?
options: Classify as viable intrauterine pregnancy
Classify as complete miscarriage
Clinical review in early pregnancy service within 24 hours, with repeat assessment as indicated
Give methotrexate solely because the rise is <63%
Discharge with routine antenatal booking
questions.rationale: A rise below 63% needs clinical review within 24 hours; hCG change alone cannot determine location.
questions.traps: The hCG threshold directs follow-up rather than diagnosing ectopic pregnancy.
questions.sourceDate: Guideline recommendations accessed 2026-11-25; original recommendation dates shown on source page

questions.stem: A 31-year-old with PUL has hCG 1,050 IU/L and a progesterone concentration of 8 nmol/L. TVUS shows neither intrauterine nor ectopic pregnancy. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Diagnose ectopic pregnancy based on progesterone
Diagnose completed miscarriage based on progesterone
Use serial hCG with clinical surveillance and safety-netting rather than progesterone to establish location
Give misoprostol immediately
Assume viable intrauterine pregnancy because hCG exceeds 1,000
questions.rationale: NICE and Egyptian Health Council advise against progesterone as an adjunct to determine location/viability in a PUL surveillance pathway.
questions.traps: Low progesterone may correlate with nonviability but cannot locate the pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old is pain-free and stable with a confirmed 24-mm tubal ectopic pregnancy, no heartbeat, hCG 780 IU/L and reliable follow-up. What is the most appropriate NICE-based offer?
options: Immediate salpingectomy is mandatory
Offer expectant management with serial hCG and explicit safety-netting
Methotrexate is mandatory regardless of preference
Repeat a home urine test in six weeks only
Offer expectant management without blood tests
questions.rationale: NICE permits expectant management for a stable pain-free woman with tubal ectopic <35 mm, no heartbeat, hCG ≤1,000 IU/L and reliable follow-up.
questions.traps: Confirmed ectopic does not automatically require intervention when strict selection criteria are met.

questions.stem: A stable woman chose expectant management for a 20-mm tubal ectopic (hCG 900 IU/L). Subsequent hCG values are 900, 830 and 825 IU/L on days 1, 2 and 4. What is the best next step?
options: Continue the same plan without review because values have fallen
Arrange senior clinical reassessment because the fall is inadequate
Discharge when hCG is below 1,000
Give progesterone to support the pregnancy
Book routine antenatal care
questions.rationale: NICE expects at least 15% fall from the previous value at day 2, 4 and 7 checks; inadequate decline warrants clinical review and senior advice.
questions.traps: A small absolute decline is not the same as the specified proportional fall.

questions.stem: A low-risk woman at 30 weeks has a singleton pregnancy. Symphysis-fundal height is below the expected trajectory at two visits; she also reports reduced fetal movements today. What is the best next step?
options: Repeat fundal height in four weeks
Urgent maternal and fetal assessment, including fetal movement evaluation and ultrasound growth/wellbeing assessment
Reassure because fundal height is a screening test
Offer routine growth scans only after 36 weeks
Start aspirin now as the sole response
questions.rationale: NICE NG201 recommends ultrasound when SFH is small; reduced movements increase urgency and require assessment.
questions.traps: The screening limitation of SFH is a reason to confirm with ultrasound, not ignore it.

questions.stem: A healthy woman with uncomplicated singleton pregnancy has normal fundal-height growth at 30 weeks and normal movements. She requests scans every two weeks to improve safety. What is the most evidence-aligned UK approach?
options: Offer fortnightly ultrasound as standard for every low-risk woman
Do not routinely offer third-trimester ultrasound after 28 weeks without an indication; continue individualised antenatal surveillance
Stop all antenatal assessments
Arrange weekly CTG because all pregnancies are at risk
Perform Doppler at every appointment
questions.rationale: NICE does not routinely recommend ultrasound after 28 weeks for uncomplicated singleton pregnancies.
questions.traps: More testing does not automatically improve outcomes in low-risk pregnancy.
questions.sourceDate: Guideline recommendations accessed 2026-11-25; original recommendation dates shown on source page
questions.sourceVerification: Official primary guideline; requires final clinical editorial review

questions.stem: A 25-week pregnant woman with chronic hypertension has repeated clinic BP 146/94 mmHg despite lifestyle advice. There is no proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction. What is the best NICE-based plan?
options: Wait until BP reaches 160/110 before any treatment
Offer an appropriate antihypertensive and aim for 135/85 mmHg
Plan immediate delivery
Prescribe diuretic solely to prevent pre-eclampsia
Avoid all BP drugs until fetal viability
questions.rationale: For chronic hypertension NICE offers treatment at sustained ≥140/90 mmHg with target 135/85 mmHg.
questions.traps: 160/110 identifies severe hypertension; it is not the threshold for all chronic hypertension treatment.
questions.sourceDate: Guideline recommendations accessed 2026-11-25; original recommendation dates shown on source page

questions.stem: A woman at 31 weeks presents with BP 168/114 mmHg, headache and visual scotomata. Platelets are 145×10⁹/L. Fetal heart is present. What is the best initial management priority?
options: Discharge with a BP diary
Admit for urgent assessment and treatment of severe hypertension, maternal stabilisation and fetal evaluation
Wait for 24-hour urine protein before acting
Repeat BP in one week
Give oral iron and review symptoms
questions.rationale: Severe hypertension with neurological symptoms requires urgent admission, antihypertensive treatment and evaluation for severe pre-eclampsia.
questions.traps: Proteinuria confirmation must not delay management of a maternal emergency.
questions.sourceDate: Guideline recommendations accessed 2026-11-25; original recommendation dates shown on source page

questions.stem: A woman at 35+4 weeks has gestational hypertension controlled at 142/92 mmHg, normal labs, reassuring fetal assessment and no other indication for delivery. What is the best UK-guideline approach?
options: Induce labour immediately because any gestational hypertension mandates birth before 37 weeks
Avoid planned early birth before 37 weeks unless other maternal or fetal indications emerge
Schedule caesarean delivery at 36 weeks
Administer magnesium sulfate routinely to all gestational hypertension cases
Ignore BP monitoring until 39 weeks
questions.rationale: NICE advises against planned birth before 37 weeks in gestational hypertension with BP <160/110 unless another indication exists.
questions.traps: Hypertension diagnosis alone does not determine immediate delivery timing.

questions.stem: At 12 weeks, a pregnant woman with systemic lupus erythematosus but no prior hypertension asks whether she qualifies for aspirin. What is the best NICE answer?
options: Only if she also has two moderate-risk factors
Yes: autoimmune disease is a high-risk factor; prescribe aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks
No: aspirin is contraindicated in all autoimmune disease
Use LMWH alone as routine pre-eclampsia prophylaxis
Start aspirin after 28 weeks
questions.rationale: Autoimmune disease such as SLE is a single high-risk factor sufficient for aspirin prophylaxis from 12 weeks.
questions.traps: Do not confuse a single high-risk factor with the multiple-moderate-factor rule.

questions.stem: A low-risk singleton pregnancy at 27 weeks has an SFH measurement concerning for small size. A growth ultrasound is normal and movements remain normal. What is the best ongoing strategy?
options: Label fetal growth restriction on the original SFH finding alone
Continue individualised antenatal care and reassess SFH at appropriate intervals; repeat imaging if new concern arises
Schedule daily Dopplers indefinitely
Deliver at 34 weeks despite reassuring findings
Ignore any later fall in SFH
questions.rationale: A single abnormal screening SFH followed by reassuring assessment does not establish FGR; continue surveillance according to risk and subsequent findings.
questions.traps: A screening concern is not equivalent to a definitive growth diagnosis.

questions.stem: A woman at 29 weeks has BP 152/98 mmHg and dipstick protein 1+. She has no severe symptoms. What is the most appropriate diagnostic step?
options: Diagnose severe pre-eclampsia based on dipstick alone
Quantify proteinuria with protein:creatinine or albumin:creatinine ratio and assess maternal/fetal status
Ignore dipstick because it is unreliable
Request 24-hour urine in every patient before any other assessment
Prescribe aspirin as definitive treatment for established hypertension
questions.rationale: NICE recommends quantifying positive dipstick proteinuria (≥1+) with PCR or ACR and interpreting results in full clinical context.
questions.traps: Dipstick screening alone should not be treated as definitive quantification.

questions.theme: Pregnancy of unknown location: select the most appropriate next management
questions.stem: Stable PUL, hCG 1,000 to 1,720 IU/L in 48 hours, mild symptoms unchanged. Which next management best follows NICE?
options: Emergency resuscitation and urgent operative assessment
Repeat serum hCG in 6 hours
Repeat serum hCG after 48 hours
TVUS in 7–14 days with safety-netting
Clinical review within 24 hours
Urine pregnancy test 14 days after second hCG
Immediate methotrexate for all cases
Serum progesterone to determine pregnancy location
Routine antenatal booking without repeat imaging
Discharge without follow-up
questions.rationale: A >63% rise suggests a developing IUP but ectopic cannot be excluded; follow-up TVUS 7–14 days, possibly earlier at hCG >=1500.
questions.traps: A normal-looking rise does not confirm location.

questions.theme: Choose the single most appropriate preconception intervention
questions.stem: A 32-year-old with type 1 diabetes, HbA1c 94 mmol/mol, is planning conception immediately. She asks for the single most important risk-based recommendation today.
options: Folic acid 400 micrograms daily
Folic acid 5 mg daily until 12 weeks
Continue an ACE inhibitor until 20 weeks
Stop statin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
Aim for HbA1c below 48 mmol/mol if safely achievable
Strongly advise against pregnancy while HbA1c exceeds 86 mmol/mol
Replace insulin with a sulfonylurea
Prescribe aspirin from the day contraception stops
Offer blood ketone testing equipment for type 1 diabetes
Delay retinal assessment until the third trimester
questions.rationale: Above 86 mmol/mol (>10%), NICE strongly advises not becoming pregnant until HbA1c is lower.
questions.traps: A folate prescription is necessary but not sufficient to address very high glycaemic risk.

questions.theme: Choose the single most appropriate preconception intervention
questions.stem: A 27-year-old with well-controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 45 mmol/mol) takes a prenatal tablet with 400 micrograms folate. She will stop contraception next month. Select the indicated supplement change.

Continue an ACE inhibitor until 20 weeks
Stop statin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
Aim for HbA1c below 48 mmol/mol if safely achievable
Strongly advise against pregnancy while HbA1c exceeds 86 mmol/mol
Replace insulin with a sulfonylurea
Prescribe aspirin from the day contraception stops
Offer blood ketone testing equipment for type 1 diabetes
Delay retinal assessment until the third trimester
questions.rationale: Diabetes requires folic acid 5 mg daily before conception through 12 weeks.
questions.traps: Good glycaemic control does not remove the high-dose folate recommendation.

questions.theme: Choose the single most appropriate preconception intervention
questions.stem: A 30-year-old with type 1 diabetes uses a pump and has episodic marked hyperglycaemia during viral illnesses. Which additional preconception self-management resource is specifically indicated?
options: Folic acid 400 micrograms daily

Continue an ACE inhibitor until 20 weeks

Aim for HbA1c below 48 mmol/mol if safely achievable

Prescribe aspirin from the day contraception stops
Offer blood ketone testing equipment for type 1 diabetes
Delay retinal assessment until the third trimester
questions.rationale: NICE advises a blood ketone meter and strips in type 1 diabetes, with testing during hyperglycaemia or illness.
questions.traps: Ketone monitoring is not replaced by HbA1c or glucose checks.

questions.theme: Choose the most appropriate plan for a woman planning pregnancy or newly pregnant
questions.stem: A 36-year-old with chronic hypertension is taking losartan and plans pregnancy. She is not yet pregnant. Select the medication action that best addresses fetal risk.
options: Continue losartan throughout pregnancy
Switch an ARB to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive
Give aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth
Begin aspirin 150 mg before conception for all nulliparous women
Offer LMWH alone to prevent pre-eclampsia
Offer aspirin only after proteinuria develops
Offer routine salt restriction to prevent pre-eclampsia
Withhold treatment of sustained BP 145/95 in chronic hypertension
Use labetalol as a possible first-line treatment for chronic hypertension in pregnancy
Offer planned birth at 34 weeks solely because chronic hypertension is controlled
questions.rationale: ARB exposure should be avoided by changing to an appropriate alternative before conception or as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.
questions.traps: Stopping all treatment without a replacement may leave uncontrolled hypertension.

questions.theme: Choose the most appropriate plan for a woman planning pregnancy or newly pregnant

questions.rationale: Prior hypertensive disease of pregnancy is a high-risk factor; NICE advises aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks until birth.
questions.traps: Do not substitute routine LMWH or start aspirin solely on a preconception schedule.

questions.theme: Select the most appropriate immediate response to changing findings in PUL
questions.stem: A patient with PUL has hCG 700 then 1260 IU/L at 48 hours, is stable, has no new pain and has access to emergency care. What follow-up best fits the trend?
options: Emergency assessment and resuscitation with urgent surgical review
Repeat quantitative serum hCG as close as possible to 48 hours
Repeat serum hCG in 6 hours
Offer TVUS in 7–14 days, with earlier scan considered if hCG >=1500
Clinical review in an early pregnancy service within 24 hours
Urine pregnancy test 14 days after the second hCG
Discharge because the hCG is below the discriminatory zone
Methotrexate based on hCG trend alone
Serum progesterone to establish pregnancy location
Routine 12-week booking without safety-net advice
questions.rationale: Rise >63% suggests a developing intrauterine pregnancy but cannot exclude ectopic; arrange follow-up TVUS in 7–14 days.
questions.traps: A reassuring rise does not confirm intrauterine location.

questions.theme: Select the most appropriate immediate response to changing findings in PUL
questions.stem: A stable patient with PUL has hCG 1100 then 1400 IU/L at 48 hours. She has unchanged mild symptoms. What is the appropriate next action?
options: Emergency assessment and resuscitation with urgent surgical review

Serum progesterone to establish pregnancy location
Routine 12-week booking without safety-net advice
questions.rationale: A rise <63% requires clinical review within 24 hours.
questions.traps: A modest rise is neither proof of ectopic pregnancy nor a reason for automatic methotrexate.

questions.theme: Select the most appropriate immediate response to changing findings in PUL

options: Emergency assessment and resuscitation with urgent surgical review

questions.rationale: New symptoms and suspected intraperitoneal bleeding override a declining hCG; urgent emergency assessment is required.
questions.traps: A falling hCG does not exclude rupture.

questions.theme: Select the best next diagnostic or management action
questions.stem: An asymptomatic woman with uncertain dates has a transvaginal scan showing an intrauterine embryo with CRL 5.5 mm and no visible heartbeat. What is the best next step?
options: Repeat TVUS after at least 7 days before diagnosing miscarriage
Diagnose miscarriage immediately from CRL 5 mm without heartbeat
Seek a second opinion and/or repeat TVUS after at least 7 days for CRL >=7 mm without heartbeat
Diagnose miscarriage from mean sac diameter 18 mm with no fetal pole
Use LMP alone to determine when heartbeat must be visible
Measure serum progesterone to prove viability
Offer immediate methotrexate for an empty uterus
Use transabdominal ultrasound alone to rule out ectopic pregnancy
Offer urgent assessment for haemodynamic instability
Discharge a symptomatic patient with no safety net
questions.rationale: With CRL <7 mm and no heartbeat, repeat TVUS after at least 7 days before making a definitive diagnosis.
questions.traps: A single scan cannot establish nonviability at this size.

questions.theme: Select the best next diagnostic or management action

Use transabdominal ultrasound alone to rule out ectopic pregnancy

Discharge a symptomatic patient with no safety net
questions.rationale: For CRL >=7 mm without heartbeat, NICE recommends second opinion and/or repeat scan after at least 7 days before diagnosing miscarriage.

questions.theme: Select the best antenatal management action
questions.stem: At 30 weeks, a woman with pre-eclampsia has sustained BP 172/114, headache and epigastric pain. What is the priority from the options?
options: Admit and promptly treat severe hypertension
Continue routine community review despite BP 170/112
Start antihypertensive therapy for sustained BP above 140/90
Give routine LMWH to prevent pre-eclampsia
Offer aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks in a high-risk pregnancy
Plan birth at 34 weeks solely for controlled chronic hypertension
Discuss timing of birth after 37 weeks with senior obstetrician if chronic hypertension remains <160/110
Give antenatal steroids to every patient with hypertension at 39 weeks
Use magnesium sulfate as sole antihypertensive
Perform no fetal assessment when pre-eclampsia is diagnosed
questions.rationale: Severe hypertension with concerning symptoms warrants admission, urgent treatment and maternal/fetal assessment.
questions.traps: Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, when indicated, is not a substitute for BP control.

questions.theme: Select the best antenatal management action

Perform no fetal assessment when pre-eclampsia is diagnosed

questions.traps: Do not wait for severe-range pressures.

questions.theme: Select the best antenatal management action

questions.traps: Neither mandatory immediate caesarean nor automatic continuation to 41 weeks is justified.

questions.theme: Choose the most appropriate response in routine antenatal care
questions.stem: At 31 weeks, an otherwise low-risk singleton has SFH measurements that have plateaued across two appropriately spaced visits. There is no current regular growth scan programme. What is the next investigation?
options: Offer ultrasound for fetal growth and wellbeing
Reassure without assessment because a previous CTG was normal
Assess the woman and fetus promptly for reduced fetal movements
Offer routine ultrasound every week to all low-risk women after 28 weeks
Continue serial SFH plotting after 24 weeks when not on growth scans
Measure SFH daily
Offer routine ultrasound after 28 weeks to all uncomplicated singletons
Use a single normal SFH to exclude FGR permanently
Consider urgency of growth ultrasound in light of reduced movements or hypertension
Ignore maternal perception of reduced movements if fetal heart auscultation is normal
questions.rationale: Small or plateauing SFH warrants ultrasound for growth and wellbeing, with urgency influenced by additional risk.
questions.traps: Auscultation alone does not establish normal growth.

questions.theme: Choose the most appropriate response in routine antenatal care

Use a single normal SFH to exclude FGR permanently
Consider urgency of growth ultrasound in light of reduced movements or hypertension
Ignore maternal perception of reduced movements if fetal heart auscultation is normal
questions.rationale: NICE advises assessment whenever movements are reduced after 24 weeks, regardless of previous reassuring testing.
questions.traps: Previous CTG does not substitute for current assessment.

questions.theme: Choose the most appropriate response in routine antenatal care
questions.stem: A low-risk singleton attends routine care at 26 weeks with normal growth history and no scheduled growth ultrasounds. Which serial bedside method is recommended?
options: Offer ultrasound for fetal growth and wellbeing
Reassure without assessment because a previous CTG was normal
Assess the woman and fetus promptly for reduced fetal movements
Offer routine ultrasound every week to all low-risk women after 28 weeks
Continue serial SFH plotting after 24 weeks when not on growth scans
Measure SFH daily
Offer routine ultrasound after 28 weeks to all uncomplicated singletons
Use a single normal SFH to exclude FGR permanently
Consider urgency of growth ultrasound in light of reduced movements or hypertension
Ignore maternal perception of reduced movements if fetal heart auscultation is normal
questions.rationale: NICE recommends SFH at each antenatal visit after 24 weeks, no more frequently than every two weeks, unless regular growth scans are occurring.
questions.traps: Weekly routine ultrasound or excessively frequent SFH measurements are not recommended.
